title: Lunchbreak: CBS Ranks NFL's Play Callers; Adrian Peterson's 2027 Hall of Fame Candidacy Evaluated - Minnesota Vikings
content:
Head Coach Kevin O'Connell and Defensive Coordinator Brian Flores are elite strategists. Zach Pereles of CBS Sports on Wednesday released Top 10 lists of offensive and defensive play-callers going into the season. The hierarchies were compiled with votes cast from 12 CBS Sports NFL experts. The inclusion of O'Connell and Flores isn't surprising. In two seasons with stability at quarterback (one starter in 2022 and 2024), O'Connell's offenses have ranked eighth and ninth in points scored per game. Pereles wrote the following about the fifth-year head coach who was tabbed as the league's No. 8 offensive play-caller: This season figures to be a crucial one for O'Connell, who has alternated excellent seasons with middling ones. He went 13-4 in his debut year with Kirk Cousins, then 7-10 when Cousins tore his Achilles, then 14-3 with Sam Darnold, then 9-8 last year while cycling through J.J. McCarthy, Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer. Pereles assumed Kyler Murray will be named the 2026 starter eventually and wrote Murray "could hold the key to getting things back on track in Minnesota, and it's a big bet for O'Connell, who will also hope to improve his team's running game." Flores, meanwhile, has a strong argument to be rated higher than his No. 5 designation. Since onboarding Flo' in 2023, the Vikings defenses have limited opponents to 20.1 points per game, which is good for third-fewest after Kansas City (18.6) and Houston (20.0). Furthermore, Flores' mad genius has resulted in opponents gaining the fewest yards per rush (3.9) and fourth-fewest yards per play (5.06). Minnesota also has produced the fifth-most takeaways (76) and sacks (141) in that timeframe. Here's what Pereles wrote about Flores as the DC prepares for his fourth season in Minnesota: After [Mike] Macdonald, defensive play-callers No. 2-5 were separated by a mere nine points, so if we're tiering them, Flores really belongs in Tier 2, even if he finished No. 5 overall. In fact, Flores received two second-place votes and three third-place votes. Flores' uber-aggressive scheme — the Vikings led the NFL in pressure rate last year — rattles many quarterbacks from the get-go. Click here to find out the rest of the 2026 NFL play-caller rankings. Football returns Thursday night with the 2026 Hall of Fame Game between Arizona and Carolina. On Saturday, former Vikings ball boy and iconic Cardinals WR Larry Fitzgerald will be immortalized in Canton, Ohio alongside LB Luke Kuechly, QB Drew Brees, RB Roger Craig (Vikings, 1992-93) and K Adam Vinatieri. The weekend and its greatness should be appreciated to the fullest. But it also gets us looking ahead. … Looking to the Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2027 — and 2026 Vikings Ring of Honor inductee Adrian Peterson. Peterson is receiving flowers from the franchise Nov. 9 this season when Minnesota hosts Buffalo on Monday Night Football in Week 9. "All Day" is eligible for his next call in 2027, and he should get it. In honor of this year's HOF enshrinement, Grant Gordon of NFL.com offered his predictions for the 2027 modern-era player selections, who he anticipates gaining entry to football immortality with Bill Belichick. View photos of Vikings Legend Adrian Peterson during his career with the team. He will be inducted into the Vikings Ring of Honor this year. Like most prognostications, Peterson was included. Gordon proved Peterson's case speaks for itself: History might hold tight to Peterson as the last running back of a bygone era. Like so many before him, and really none since, Peterson was a back viewed as the best player in the league for a time and just as vital to success as the guy handing him the ball. Sixteen running backs have won the AP NFL Most Valuable Player award, but Peterson's 2012 MVP was just the fourth this century, and the last, for a RB. Considering Saquon Barkley posed a 2,000-yard argument in 2024 and finished a distant No. 3 in the voting, Peterson could be the last RB to win MVP for a very long time — if not ever. Peterson ranks fifth all-time in rushing yards (14,918) and fifth in rushing TDs (120). Those numbers warrant a gold jacket, as do his seven Pro Bowls, four first-team All-Pro nods and other hardware (2007 Offensive Rookie of the Year, 2012 Offensive Player of the Year). Gordon also predicted T Willie Anderson, TE Rob Gronkowski, WR Torry Holt and TE Jason Witten to receive bronze busts in the 2027 Class, and he flagged nine others as notable modern-era candidates: G Jahri Evans, RB Frank Gore, QB Eli Manning, QB Ben Roethlisberger, CB Richard Sherman, WR Steve Smith, Sr., WR Reggie Wayne, DB Darren Woodson and OL Marshal Yanda. Excitement was in the air Wednesday morning as the Georgia Southern football team hit the field at the Tippins Center for the first of 25 preseason practices before the Eagles host Charleston Southern Sept. 5. “I can't tell you how important these 25 opportunities in the month of August are for us in preparing for that opening game and for a season,” said coach Clay Helton. “This is a team of depth. You can see it in the first practice, but it's also 46 newcomers that are learning to play together and develop chemistry together.” Among the groups needing to build chemistry, the Eagles have 11 new starters on offense. How they end up gelling together could be the difference in a good and a great team. “We've got a lot of work to do offensively,” Helton said. “You can see the talent's there but there's going to be some growing pains in camp and we've got to push really hard offensively. It's hard to replace 11 starters, but that's our job. We don't make excuses, we find answers. Those guys will progress each and every day and you can see them progress from spring. We've put in a lot of work through spring and summer. We can see a little bit of it right now going in the right direction, but there’s still a lot of work. If I'm being real, there's a lot of work to do.” Among the first-year starters on offense is North Carolina transfer quarterback Max Johnson. Johnson could be the key to the Eagles' success on offense and has been trying to bond with his teammates on and off the field. "They lived together over the summer,” Helton said. “We had eight weeks of training together. In July we threw every week with the guys. They would bring them out individually and be able to get that work. Obviously, we have our player-run practices, our walkthroughs, and they did a really nice job. You can tell they are ahead of where they were in spring.” Johnson hasn’t played a full season of football since 2021 but says he feels as healthy as he ever has and is excited about the chance to put his injuries behind him and play a complete season. “The injuries I have had have been freak accidents,” Johnson said. “It wasn’t like a pulled hamstring, it has all been some kind of broken bones. I have put my body in the best shape I can be. I am down to four percent body fat and my speed is back to where it was before my injuries. I think that is a testament to people here at Georgia Southern.” One of those people Johnson was referring to was strength and conditioning coach James Heiss who many players thanked for helping them gain muscle and speed. The Eagles have had some injury issues over the past few seasons and Helton believes some of that will be helped by the kind of shape the players are currently in. “I challenged coach Heiss and his staff to make the biggest, strongest team, and most importantly, the fastest team that we've had,” Helton said. “When I look at the bodies, yes, they're big, but they're athletic and fast. "We went out and invested in the Catapult system which has wearable technology to track data. It costs money to be able to gauge, from a technology standpoint, how far our guys are running and how explosive their workload is that they're getting every day. It then allows us to train test so you're not having to do 40’s one time a day, one time a summer. "You're actually seeing every time they get out in a workout. We had 82 personal bests since they've been at Georgia Southern as far as speed-wise. We had four guys over 22 miles per hour, 30 guys over 21 miles per hour and 72 guys over 20. It's really an explosive team.”

title: Spotlight Series Turns Lens on G.S. Hill - yesterdaysisland.com
content: The Artists Association of Nantucket (AAN) continues its Spotlight Series at the Champion Gallery in the Visual Arts Center (VAC), 24 Amelia Drive, with an exhibition featuring island artist G.S. Hill alongside Rose Gonnella, and Jennifer Rosenthal. Hill’s portion of the show offers a look at an artist whose career on Nantucket spans more than four decades and four distinct mediums. For his Spotlight Series exhibition, Hill made a deliberate choice: rather than presenting a single body of work, he wanted visitors to see the full breadth of his art. “I wanted to show the four mediums I work in: oils, watercolors, pencil drawings, and a hand-pulled etching,” he explained. The result is a show that traces the arc of his artistic development while showcasing his range of talent in one curated space. The oils and watercolors on view are contemporary pieces, drawn from his current body of work. For this exhibit, he selected different Nantucket scenes from his oeuvre, giving visitors a sense of how the island has shaped his eye over the years. His oils are serene and rich in color, while his watercolors lean classic and bright. Hill once worked in watercolor more frequently and, after some time away from it, is now returning to this medium. The pencil drawings carry particular historical weight. Created in the 1980s, they belong to the same series as pieces the Nantucket Historical Association (NHA) acquired for its permanent collection — a distinction that makes Hill the only living artist represented in the NHA’s permanent collection. “The two in the VAC show are the last of that series,” he noted. Rounding out the exhibition is a hand-pulled etching from 1983: the artist’s proof of Brant Point. It holds special significance as Hill’s final etching of the subject, and one of the last he ever created. He no longer works in that medium. G. S. Hill’s connection to the Artists Association of Nantucket goes back to the very beginning of his time on-island. “The first thing we did in 1979 when we moved to Nantucket was to join the Artists Association,” he said. “It’s part of the community.” That relationship has shaped his view of the organization’s value to artists. “Having the Artists Association of Nantucket is 100% helpful to us artists: a lot of well-known island artists got their start taking classes at AAN,” Hill commented. He also spoke highly of the Visual Arts Center as a venue for this particular show, saying “I think the VAC’s Champion Gallery is a great place to show! It is a totally different venue [from their gallery on Federal Street]. AAN has so much to offer there: classes, workshops, talks…” “Supporting local artists is important,” added AAN Board President Laurie Champion, “they are the fabric that enriches a community… It doesn’t matter if you work here or are a visitor, art talks to you. It brings people together as a community and makes people feel connected.” Laurie and her husband, Bob, are avid art collectors and have long supported Nantucket’s culture life with philanthropy, inspiration, and dedicated leadership. She founded AAN’s Wet Paint Dinner and has chaired the AAN Gala several times. “The first thing I ever bought [on Nantucket] was a set of prints by Donn Russell— I still have them,” Champion reminisced. “Every year I acquire something that will stay a part of my family. The AAN members are phenomenal…This is our first summer of Spotlight shows, and coming up is Greg Hill: he’s a legacy artist with a Lifetime Achievement Award, one of just two given that great honor and well-deserved. “Last year we (AAN) sold the one gallery and moved into the Federal Street Gallery: it has been a tremendous success…Many artists suggested that they’d like to have more than one image in a show, and it was decided that a Spotlight Show would be a good way to do that,” Champion explained. The Spotlight Series gives AAN member artists an additional opportunity to exhibit a curated collection of their work, offering visitors a broader representation of an artist’s vision than any single piece could provide. The concept grew out of discussions within AAN’s Exhibitions and Gallery Committee, with a clear goal: to enhance the visibility of AAN’s artists. The opportunity to be featured was opened to all current AAN members, who responded to a questionnaire indicating their interest and availability. From those responses, AAN organized six two-week Spotlight show slots for the year. The format allows artists to present work that might not typically appear in a standard gallery exhibition: pieces reflecting personal experiences, travels, and inspirations that extend beyond Nantucket. Each participating artist is also given the chance to share biographical information and other materials, giving visitors deeper insight into their background, process, and artistic vision. Because the Visual Arts Center also houses AAN’s Education Department and welcomes youth and adult students throughout the week, the venue extends participating artists’ reach well beyond a traditional gallery audience, creating new opportunities for a wider community to experience and engage with their work. The Spotlight Series supports several goals: helping artist members gain visibility, showcasing the depth and diversity of their work, and strengthening the bond between artists and the community. By encouraging artists to share their personal stories and creative processes alongside their work, the Spotlight Series helps the public develop a deeper appreciation for the people behind the art. Given the strong response to the 2026 series, AAN plans to continue hosting Spotlight Series shows in the Champion Gallery. The show featuring G.S. Hill, Rose Gonnella, and Jennifer Rosenthal continues to August 17. The Spotlight Series show following opens August 18 and will feature Cathy Aguiar, Kelly Broderick, and Rika Petrova-Powers. The final Spotlight show of the season includes James Dolph, Bill Hoenk, and Anne Troutman, and it opens September 1. AAN’s Champion Gallery is located within their Visual Arts Center24 Amelia Drive • NantucketArts.org • 508-228-0722

The description of a wide-ranging run across equities and bond trading landed at a moment when capital-markets activity has been thawing and advisory mandates have grown more active, placing the firm near the center of a shifting Wall Street narrative. The financial sector gathers a broad mix of enterprises that move money, price capital, and underwrite economic activity. Within that span, Goldman Sachs sits toward the capital-markets end, where trading, underwriting, and advisory work shape the earnings picture more than steady lending does. That orientation means the firm tends to reflect the mood of markets quickly, expanding when volumes rise and activity broadens, and cooling when dealmaking slows. The current stretch, marked by heavier trading flows and a firmer pipeline of transactions, plays to that character. It also underscores how the company differs from lenders whose fortunes lean more on the spread between what they pay for funding and what they charge to lend. Goldman Sachs organizes its work around global banking and markets, asset and wealth management, and a set of platform activities that connect the firm to a wider base of clients. The banking and markets arm handles trading across asset classes and advises on mergers, capital raising, and financing. The asset and wealth arm oversees money for institutions and individuals, drawing steadier fee-based revenue that can cushion the swings inherent in trading. Together these lines give the company a mix of activity that is sensitive to markets yet anchored by recurring mandates. The firm has spent recent periods sharpening that structure, trimming ventures that sat outside its core and concentrating on areas where scale and relationships compound. The freshest thread centers on trading. Desks across equities and bond markets have handled brisk volumes as markets churned around record levels, and that activity has helped keep the markets business humming. Alongside the trading story, the asset arm has been building tools that reach clients through digital channels, widening the ways the firm distributes strategies. Reports have also linked the company to interest in select private-market assets, a reminder that the firm continues to look for ways to deploy capital and expertise beyond its traditional footprint. Each thread points to a house leaning into activity rather than waiting for conditions to settle. Across the capital-markets landscape, the tone has grown more constructive. A stretch of muted dealmaking has given way to a steadier flow of mergers, financings, and public listings, and heightened market movement has kept trading desks busy. Rival houses have described similar patterns, which points to a broad rather than firm-specific shift. For a company weighted toward these activities, that backdrop matters, because a thicker pipeline of transactions tends to feed several revenue lines at once. The breadth of the current pickup, touching both trading and advisory work, marks a change from the leaner conditions that prevailed when issuance was scarce and caution ran high. The wider market has been dominated by enthusiasm around artificial intelligence, with a handful of technology names carrying indexes toward record ground before a modest pullback. That concentration has shaped how capital moves and how banks price and place new issues. Heavy activity in technology financing, hedging, and structured trades tends to flow through the desks of the largest houses, and Goldman Sachs counts among them. At the same time, gold has climbed to fresh peaks and energy markets have swung on geopolitical headlines, adding to the volume of trades that flow across the firm's platforms. A market this active, even when it wobbles, generally keeps intermediaries occupied. Several currents run through the financial group at once. Capital-markets desks have benefited from firmer issuance and livelier trading, while wealth and asset managers have leaned on fee-based revenue that grows with client assets. There has also been a steady push toward technology, as firms weave data tools and automation through trading, client service, and back-office work. Goldman Sachs has aligned with these currents, expanding fee-driven activity while spending on the platforms that carry trades and advice to clients. The blend of cyclical market activity and steadier management fees is a recurring theme across the sector, and the company's structure reflects an attempt to balance the two. Goldman Sachs positions itself as a house built for scale and complexity, the kind of firm large institutions and corporations turn to for demanding transactions. That standing rests on deep relationships, a global footprint, and the capacity to commit capital when clients need it. The firm has worked to pair that market-facing muscle with the steadier ballast of asset and wealth management, aiming to smooth the swings that come with a trading-heavy mix. The strategy is to be indispensable at the moments that matter most to clients, whether that means executing a difficult trade, financing an acquisition, or shepherding a company to public markets, while building recurring fee streams alongside. Day to day, the company concentrates on managing the mechanics of committing capital, funding, and client service with discipline. Trading desks calibrate exposure across fast-moving markets, financing teams line up capital for deals, and the asset arm tends the money entrusted to it. Underpinning all of this is a heavy spending on technology, from the systems that route and settle trades to the analytics that inform pricing. The firm has also emphasized cost control, pruning activities that did not fit and channeling resources toward areas of strength. This operational tightening aims to let the company capture busy periods without letting expenses run ahead of activity. The capital-markets model carries built-in swings. When issuance dries up or trading quiets, revenue can fall quickly, and the firm's tilt toward these activities makes it sensitive to shifts in sentiment. Oversight adds another dimension, as large financial institutions operate under close regulatory attention and must keep ample capital against their activities. Competition is fierce, with rival houses chasing the same mandates and pressing on fees. Broader pressures, from the path of interest rates to geopolitical flare-ups, can reshape conditions with little warning. Navigating this terrain calls for steady management of exposure and a willingness to lean in when activity picks up and pull back when it fades. Goldman Sachs competes against a cluster of large lenders and pure-play advisory firms, each vying for trading flow, underwriting mandates, and advisory roles. The largest universal banks pair market activities with vast deposit bases, while boutique advisers compete on relationships and specialization. Goldman Sachs has long carved out a place near the top of league tables for dealmaking, a standing it defends by combining reach, expertise, and the capacity to commit capital. Its expansion into asset and wealth management brings it up against dedicated money managers as well. The result is a crowded field in which the firm relies on scale and reputation to stay in contention for the most demanding work. Set against a market that pushed to records before easing back, the financial group has drawn a mixed reception, with capital-markets names leaning on activity levels while lenders weigh the path of rates. Goldman Sachs, sitting at the market-facing end of the US financial stocks, tends to move with the rhythm of trading and dealmaking rather than the slow grind of lending margins. The recent cooling in headline indexes has done little to quiet the flows that cross the firm's desks, since volatility itself generates activity. That dynamic helps explain why a banner trading run can coincide with a softer tone in the broad tape. A defining feature of large financial houses is the attention paid to capital strength and funding. Goldman Sachs manages a sizable balance sheet, calibrating how much capital backs its trading and financing activities and how it funds those positions. Regulators expect ample buffers, and the firm has framed its capital management around meeting those expectations while distributing cash to owners through dividends and buybacks. This balancing act, deploying capital to earn while keeping enough in reserve to weather stress, is central to how the company operates. It also shapes the pace at which the firm can lean into busy markets without stretching its resources. Much of the firm's standing rests on the depth of its client relationships. Large corporations, institutions, and governments turn to Goldman Sachs at moments that demand experience and reach, whether raising capital, executing a merger, or managing exposure across markets. Those relationships tend to compound over time, as clients that engage the firm for one mandate often come back for others. The wealth arm extends the same logic to individuals and families, aiming to serve a client across a lifetime of needs. Cultivating and defending these relationships is a constant effort, because rivals chase the same clients, and reputation, discretion, and consistent execution weigh heavily in who wins the most demanding work. Technology has grown central to how the firm operates and competes. The systems that route, price, and settle trades must handle enormous volume with precision, and the analytics that inform decisions draw on vast pools of data. Goldman Sachs has committed heavily to these tools, aiming to run its markets business efficiently while extending digital reach through its asset and platform activities. The push toward automation and data-driven service touches trading, client interaction, and back-office work alike. Keeping pace with technological change is a running requirement across the sector, and the firm has framed much of its spending around staying at the front of that effort rather than falling behind nimble rivals. A defining feature of the firm is its global footprint. Goldman Sachs operates across major financial centers, connecting clients to markets and capital around the world. That reach lets it move activity to wherever conditions are busiest and to serve clients with cross-border needs, an advantage that smaller or more regional houses struggle to match. Global scale also brings complexity, as the firm must navigate different rules, currencies, and market structures. The company has treated its international presence as a core strength, using it to capture activity wherever it arises and to offer clients a single house capable of executing demanding work across geographies and asset classes. The wider economic backdrop feeds directly into how a market-facing house fares. The path of interest rates shapes financing costs and the appetite for dealmaking, while the tone of markets governs how readily companies raise capital and how actively clients trade. Signs of thawing issuance and firmer trading, set against a market that reached record ground before easing, point to conditions that have grown more constructive for the activities Goldman Sachs handles. Yet those signals can shift quickly, as sentiment turns on economic data, geopolitical headlines, and the mood around the technology theme driving much of the market. The firm reads these currents constantly, calibrating how aggressively to lean into activity and how much capital to commit, a discipline that sits at the core of running a business tied so closely to the rhythm of markets. Because so much of the firm's activity moves with market conditions, its path tends to track the broader cycle. Busy markets and active dealmaking lift trading and advisory revenue, while quiet stretches weigh on them. The company has sought to soften those swings by building recurring fee streams and managing costs with discipline, aiming to earn well when activity is strong without overextending when it fades. The current stretch of firmer trading and thawing dealmaking sits on the constructive side of that cycle. How long such conditions last remains uncertain, and the firm's structure is built to flex with the rhythm rather than to depend on any single set of conditions persisting. For those following the company, the threads worth watching center on whether the current pickup in trading and dealmaking endures, how the asset and wealth arm grows its base of recurring fees, and how the firm balances market-facing activity against steadier lines. The interplay between a technology-led market and the financing and hedging that flow to large houses will continue to shape activity. Set against the [Dow Jones Industrial Average], where Goldman Sachs carries meaningful weight, the firm's fortunes offer a window into the health of Wall Street's engine. title: The BMW That Has Gold Wing Owners Rethinking Long-Distance Touring - Top Speed
content: For a long time, traditional full-dressers have set the standard for luxury long-distance touring on two wheels. Harley-Davidson and Indian lead the pack with luxury galore and top-spec components. And metric luxury tourer options like the Honda Gold Wing do one better by offering more sophisticated technology for a relatively affordable price tag. Now, though, there's a new threat to this segment: large-capacity versatile adventure tourers. Not only do these ADVs offer similar levels of riding comfort, convenience, and luxury features, but they also edge ahead with added off-roading finesse. Want a reliable used luxury ADV tourer? Then, we have a definitive and affordable winner that will make you want to ditch your Gold Wing. This article has been updated with more information on the bike's legacy. Traditional touring bikes (especially the full dresser options) have nailed the formula to offer the most comfortable, luxurious, and stress-free cross-country riding experience. But versatility isn't their strong suit. Life on endless paved roads is great until a bad stretch or tight spaces come into the picture. Enter ADV tourers. They make a better case by offering more than 90 percent of a full-dresser's experience in a much lighter and more versatile package. Manufacturers BMW, Ducati, and Triumph particularly deserve credit for this, as they offer a long-distance version of their versatile, flagship ADVs with a bigger fuel tank and more mile-munching-focused comfort and convenience features. They come with relatively smaller road-focused wheels, less suspension travel, and more luggage space. Their off-roading capabilities are reduced, but they are still a lot better than what a low-slung full-dresser would offer. While new 2026 models are already impressive, we have a gold mine of used touring-ready adventure bikes at our disposal, too. If we pick the right one with impressive reliability and after-sales support, then a luxury touring experience can be had for as much as half the price of a new full-dresser. Thankfully, we don't have to look far because the BMW R 1250 GS Adventure fits this bill perfectly. The prime example of this is a used R 1250 GS Adventure. The standard R 1250 GS is already a great all-rounder. But the Adventure model takes things further, becoming a formidable luxury touring bike alternative. The GSA has a much larger 7.9-gallon fuel tank and more suspension travel. It comes standard with heavy-duty engine and tank crash bars, auxiliary lights, wider footpegs, a larger windscreen, and stainless steel luggage mounts for aluminum panniers. Thus, the 1250 GSA offers nearly 90 percent of the experience with the added advantage of scaling over rocky terrain with ease. The huge fuel tank should translate to an easy 350+ mile range (claimed fuel economy rating is ~47 miles per gallon). Then, we have the prices. Currently, the last-gen R 1250 GS models (2020 to 2023) are being sold for as low as $16,500 on the used marketplaces. We even stumbled upon a used 2024 model for under $17,000, which is a pretty good deal. Oh, and while BMW has replaced the R 1250 GS with the new tech-loaded R 1300 GS, the predecessor still packs enough punch to stand tall in 2026. In fact, a used R 1250 GS actually offers more value than the R 1300 GS, if you are unfazed by the intimidating dimensions of the former. Touring motorcycles claim to take you around the world, but they only go as far as the blacktop does. Once the pavement ends, it’s the adventure bikes that carry the baton of exploration forward. And few motorcycles do it quite like the BMW GS. It’s the reason why the GS has become the go-to full-size adventure bike for those wanting to explore the world on two wheels. And the R 1250 GSA represents that persona better than any other GS. As far as used previous-generation GS motorcycles are concerned, the liquid-cooled GS models are the most advanced used GS models you can find for a bargain. The trend started with the 2013 R 1200 GS, which was the first full-size GS to feature the new liquid-cooled boxer engine. It also brought semi-active Dynamic ESA suspension, five riding modes, a quickshifter, keyless ignition, cornering ABS, and much more, depending on the package and model year. It was a milestone in the ADV segment. In 2019, the R 1200 GS was replaced by the 2019 R 1250 GS and GSA, which was at the time the most advanced adventure bike in the segment. It featured a larger engine with ShiftCam tech, producing impressive power and torque in all riding conditions. It also got a large TFT display, Multi-Controller wheel, hill start assist, and much more, depending on spec. In the used market, the GSA remains among the most capable and advanced adventure tourers you can buy even in 2026. The BMW GS was already hugely successful, and it reached an even wider audience thanks to Ewan McGregor and Charlie Boorman during their adventures documented in the Long Way Round and Long Way Down series. Over the years, the GS has only built on that reputation, cementing itself as the ultimate globe-trotter for explorers. And while older airhead GS models are iconic, it’s the R 1250 GSA that represents that globe-trotting character better than any other. Picking this bike up today means you’re buying one of the most influential ADVs ever made, not just a bike that’s comfortable for the long haul. The R 1250 GSA packs a proven liquid-cooled 1,254 cc boxer twin engine with 136 horsepower at 7,750 RPM and 105 pound-feet of torque at 6,250 RPM. Power is sent to the rear wheel via a six-speed manual and a final shaft drive system. All the low-end oomph helps with its relaxed yet sprinty highway touring capabilities. The BMW badge might persuade you into thinking the GS is an expensive bike to maintain. That, however, is not the case because long service intervals help keep the GS up and about for longer. Upholding its globe-trotting ability is its durable build quality all around. BMW specifies an oil change every 6,000 miles or once a year, whichever comes first. The valve clearance checks are reserved for every 12,000 miles. Furthermore, the shaft drive eliminates the need to replace sprockets and tighten and lube a chain every few hundred miles. The shaft drive does need an inspection every 12,500 miles and a preventive replacement at 60,000 miles. This could become an expensive affair, but thankfully, BMW covers the shaft replacement for the lifetime of the vehicle at no cost to the owner. This benefit wasn't extended to the new R 1300 GS, making the 1250 GS more desirable on the ownership front. The R 1250 GSA is underpinned by a two-section frame consisting of the main frame and a bolt-on rear frame, with the mill being a stressed member here. The frame sits on a unique suspension setup: BMW's 37 mm Telelever setup with a central spring strut and BMW's Paralever assembly with a spring strut attached to a cast aluminum single-sided swing arm. The Telelever front setup is famed for offering a high level of anti-dive under hard braking and also elevates confidence when going fast or over rough terrain. The GSA electronic suspension control (optional when new) further helps with automatic damping and load compensation based on riding modes. This electronic control helps this nearly 600-pound tall-riding ADV behave as a stable highway runner, a commendable off-roader, and even a nimble mountain-road companion. As for the cockpit, there's a crisp TFT with smartphone connectivity. It enables access to a slew of standard safety, assistive, and convenience features, including Dynamic Traction Control, lean-sensitive ABS, Hill Start Control, and three ride modes (Eco, Rain, and Road). The optional suite is also solid, with the aforementioned Dynamic Electronic Suspension Adjustment with automatic load leveling, Riding Mode Pro with additional modes (Dynamic, Dynamic Pro, Enduro, and Enduro Pro), Automated Hill Start Control Pro, Dynamic Brake Assist, and Engine Brake Control. The best part about used motorcycles is that all of these optional features can be bundled for much less than the original price. Most used R 1250 GS specimens often come stacked with all optional features. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. content: Globally we expect GDP growth to slow in 2026 amid lingering headwinds from the rise in energy prices. In the US, we see growth near 2% with the AI boom supporting business investment and contributing nearly 0.5pp to consumer spending through equity wealth effects. We see AI-driven above trend growth in EMs as well, but below-trend growth in developed markets ex-US. Core inflation has undershot in recent months and now stands at 2.1% in the G10 ex-US, despite energy prices surging in March. In the US, we expect core inflation closer to 3% in December 2026 given the effects of tariffs, energy prices, and AI measurement issues, with it falling closer to 2% in 2027 as those subside. The usual rationale for raising rates is to prevent economic overheating by bringing aggregate demand into balance with supply. The challenge for central banks today is that most inflation is supply driven and rate policy becomes a less effective tool. As such, we expect the Fed to hold for evidence of price passthrough and the Bank of England to watch the labor market, while the European Central Bank may still hike in September to guard inflation expectations. From a top-down perspective, index performance has been strong this year and global markets are within striking distance of all-time highs. Under the surface, rapid rotations have challenged portfolio stability. AI has been at the epicenter, with trade-offs emerging between software vs hardware and hyperscalers vs infrastructure providers. Low correlation and high dispersion markets are ideal conditions for alpha generation, in our view, with a preference for quality earnings and balance sheets. Significant AI capex requires a mix of financing, with hyperscaler issuance accounting for 16-23% of gross issuance in USD IG, HY, and leveraged loan markets YTD, and a growing share of non-USD and private markets as well. Technology spreads have widened, in part reflecting heavy supply, but credit fundamentals appear reasonable – particularly for the top of the capital stack. The sharp increase in US rates and strong US equity performance has given legs to the dollar rally, even as geopolitical and energy risks have normalized. title: Goldman's AI Strategy: Transforming Operations & Unlocking New Growth - The Globe and Mail
content: The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.GS is pursuing an ambitious, firmwide artificial intelligence (AI) transformation aimed at expanding fee-based revenues, improving productivity and strengthening long-term operating leverage. The initiative spans trading, investment banking, asset and wealth management, and internal operations, positioning AI as both an efficiency tool and a potential growth catalyst. Last month, Yahoo Finance, citing Reuters, reported that Goldman Sachs Asset Management had launched AlphaAI, an artificial intelligence-focused investment platform. The initiative underscores the firm's conviction that AI will emerge as a significant driver of investment opportunities and returns across both public and private markets. Earlier, Goldman also partnered with Anthropic on a $1.5-billion initiative designed to accelerate AI adoption across hundreds of portfolio companies. At the center of Goldman’s transformation are two major initiatives — One Goldman Sachs 3.0, or OneGS 3.0, and the GS AI Assistant program. OneGS 3.0 is a multi-year effort to integrate AI into the firm’s core operating model rather than treat it as a standalone technology. The program focuses on simplifying workflows, modernizing infrastructure and supporting scalable growth through shared platforms, standardized processes and higher-quality data. The GS AI Assistant is expected to further improve employee productivity by helping professionals analyze information, generate content and complete routine tasks more efficiently. As adoption expands, the platform could reduce manual workloads and allow employees to devote more time to client engagement, decision-making and higher-value activities. Beyond operational improvements, AI is reshaping Goldman’s revenue mix. The firm is increasingly focusing on higher-fee, data-driven businesses while reducing the reliance on balance sheet-intensive activities. Its acquisition of Industry Ventures underscores this shift, with plans to leverage AI and advanced analytics to enhance valuation, risk assessment and portfolio construction in private markets. Management has expressed strong confidence in AI’s long-term potential. Although spending on AI, data and digital infrastructure may keep expenses elevated in the near term, the investments could generate meaningful productivity gains and help the firm move toward its medium-term efficiency ratio target of 60%. Goldman’s peers JPMorgan JPM and Citigroup C are investing heavily in AI, automation and digital transformation to improve efficiency, personalize services and maintain a competitive advantage. JPMorgan is embedding AI across fraud detection, credit risk, wealth management and operations to enhance efficiency, compliance and customer experience. Generative AI tools further streamline workflows, strengthening JPMorgan’s leadership in U.S. digital banking. Citigroup is accelerating its AI transformation by modernizing legacy systems, deploying chatbots and advancing agentic AI for complex financial tasks. Citigroup’s strategy spans wealth management, corporate banking and real-time lending, supported by strong digital engagement and seamless omnichannel services.
